source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in chess
finding: Founding study. Master, Class A player and beginner did a copy task (board in view) and a 5 s recall task. Glances and pauses over 2 s were used to cut the reconstruction into chunks. Chunk size grew with skill; the number of chunks stayed inside the 7+-2 span.
numbers: N=3 players (one per level). Middle-game recall: first-chunk size 3.8 (M), 2.6 (A), 2.4 (B) pieces. Number of chunks also rose with skill, so the claim 'same number of chunks at all skills' was NOT supported. Master first-trial recall 62% vs A 34% vs B 18%.
quote: a master encodes information about a position in chunks
limits: One subject per level; tiny sample. Positions partly from non-master games; master recall (16 of 25 pieces) was lower than de Groot's 23-24.
agent_relevance: Chunking = learned units that cost one memory slot each. Memory design: store and retrieve in meaningful units, not raw tokens.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in chess: random positions and replication of de Groot
finding: On randomized positions there was no relation between memory and playing strength. On nine fresh quiet master-game positions the three players matched de Groot's results.
numbers: 5 s recall of new positions: B 33%, A 49%, M 81%. Earlier positions first trial: B 18%, A 34%, M 62%. Master recognised 4 of 9 positions within 1 s, yet recall was 83% (recognised) vs 79% (not): recognising the game did not help.
limits: Replication of de Groot is by the same N=3. Random positions later shown to keep a small skill edge (a10, a14, a15).
agent_relevance: Expert advantage depends on structure that matches stored patterns. Scrambled or unfamiliar input removes it. Test the agent's memory on structured vs scrambled context.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) 2 s latency criterion and chess relations
finding: Chunks were defined as runs of pieces placed with under 2 s between them. Pairs of pieces inside a chunk shared many more chess relations (attack, defence, colour, type, proximity) than pairs across a boundary.
numbers: Latency distributions had a tail of long intervals; short intervals (<2 s) co-occurred with many relations. 77 chunks of two or more pieces from the master over five middle-game positions; over 75% fell in three types (castled king, pawn chains, other familiar clusters).
limits: Operational definition of a chunk, not a direct observation. Later work (a05) shows it is robust but chunks may be larger.
agent_relevance: Gives a measurable chunk definition: a bounded cluster with strong internal relations. Useful for judging whether an agent's memory items are real units.

source: Simon & Chase (1973) Skill in chess, American Scientist
finding: Popular statement of the theory plus the MAPP simulation (EPAM-based with PERCEIVER eye movements). Estimated a master needs about 50,000 chunks, from the argument that P^7 must exceed the number of possible positions N.
numbers: Masters/grandmasters ~93% correct on ~25-piece positions; experts ~72%; Class A about half; novices ~8 pieces (~33%). MAPP with ~1,000 patterns performed about like a Class A player, twice a beginner, half a master; it got 51% of the pieces the master placed and 30% of those the master missed. Chunk learning ~5-8 s per chunk; STM ~7 chunks. If P=50,000 then P^7 is about 8x10^32.
limits: 50,000 is an order-of-magnitude estimate, later disputed (Holding said 2,500, a26) and defended (a12).
agent_relevance: A working computer model of how a store of chunks yields expert recall; sets scale expectations (tens of thousands of units, not hundreds).

source: Gobet & Simon (1998) Expert chess memory: revisiting the chunking hypothesis
finding: Replicated the Chase & Simon copy and recall method with a computer display (no hand-grasp limit) and 26 players. Latency and relation patterns matched the 1973 data closely, so the 2 s chunk boundary is robust. But chunks were much larger than in 1973, which pushed the theory toward templates.
numbers: N=26 male players, Elo 1680-2510 (mean 2078, SD 233). Masters n=5. Largest chunk (median per position): Masters 16.8 pieces in recall, 14 in copy, vs 7 for the 1973 master. Random positions: 6.3 pieces (copy) and 4.6 (recall) at all skill levels. Correlations with Chase & Simon relation probabilities: within-glance copy r>.89; copy game within-glance .81; recall game short latencies .86.
limits: Apparatus differs (mouse and screen). Authors give reasons for larger chunks: hand capacity in 1973, better players, different positions. A partial replication with a changed size estimate.
agent_relevance: Chunks may be much bigger than 4-5 items and may be schema-like. For an agent: size of the retrievable unit matters more than count of items held.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards (Experiment 1)
finding: Recall of 1 to 5 boards, 5 s each. Experts recalled far more pieces than the original theory allows (7 chunks x 4-5 pieces). Proposed templates: big chunks with a stable core and slots that fill quickly.
numbers: N=13 (Masters, Experts, Class A). Masters replaced up to 60 pieces, Experts ~40. Chunks: 2.3 (1 board) to 9.9 (5 boards) for Experts and Masters; Class A 2.2 to 4.5. Median first-piece latency (Masters) 3.1 s with one board vs 6.0 s with several. Random positions: Masters 21%, Experts 16%, Class A 12% (ns, F(2,10)=3.46).
limits: Small N per group. The grandmaster lost one trial through inattention (Masters at 5 boards 50% if removed). Chunk counts depend on the 2 s rule.
agent_relevance: Retrieve a template (stable core) and fill variable slots instead of re-reading everything. Maps to structured memory records with fields.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: interference studies reanalysed
finding: Reanalysed older interference and depth-of-processing studies. Charness (1976) found only 6-8% fewer pieces after a 30 s filled delay. Frey & Adesman (1976) need no theory change once 8 s per chunk learning time is counted.
numbers: Charness decrease 6-8% (vs large loss for trigrams). Frey & Adesman: ~10 pieces per position for two positions; chunk arithmetic: two 3-piece chunks stored in 16 s plus 7 slots of 2 pieces gives about 20 pieces. Goldin and Frey & Adesman level-of-processing effects are confounded with study time.
limits: Charness's long first-piece latency was said not to have been replicated at the time.
agent_relevance: A long-term store explains robustness to interference. Memory placed outside the volatile context resists distraction; test with distractor insertions.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: one expert trained to recall many boards (Experiment 3)
finding: A chessmaster trained for months with a mnemonic cue list and raised the number of boards recalled at over 70% accuracy to nine, replacing up to 160 pieces correctly. Template theory says he added slots and labels, not STM capacity.
numbers: Baseline without cue list: 4 boards 50% and 55%; 5 boards 54.3%; 2 boards 79.9% (~40 pieces). Peak nine boards (block 18), then eight (blocks 19-22) and seven (23-30). Criterion: no more than one board under 60%.
limits: N=1. The gain came from a deliberate retrieval structure, so it mixes template and mnemonic effects.
agent_relevance: Explicit index labels per stored item can multiply capacity. Supports keyed memory with cheap labels.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates: slot-filling parameters
finding: Template theory: some chunks evolve into structures with slots. Filling a slot takes under 1 s; learning a new chunk takes 8 s; one template pointer per board sits in STM, so the limit is about 7+-2 boards.
numbers: Slot fill <1 s (derived <=2 s per slot at >=60% accuracy). New-chunk learning 8 s; familiarisation 2 s.
limits: Parameters are inherited from EPAM fits, not refit to chess.
agent_relevance: Fast write into pre-built slots vs slow creation of new structure: a design rule for memory write cost.

source: Gobet & Simon (2000) Five seconds or sixty? Presentation time in expert memory
finding: Recall of chess positions with presentation times 1 to 60 s in three skill groups. Both the amount learned in 1 s and the later rate rise with skill, for game and random positions.
numbers: N=20 (Masters 5, Experts 8, Class A 7, Elo 1770-2595). Fit P=100-B*exp(-c(t-1)): game positions B=75.2 (A), 66.4 (Exp), 29.2 (Masters); c=0.033, 0.074, 0.435. Random: B=90.6, 85.3, 80.5; c=0.006, 0.012, 0.018. Masters ~92.4% at 10 s. Masters at 1 s about equal Experts at 10 s.
limits: Masters' fit r2 only .35 for games (ceiling, spread); Masters got no game positions over 10 s.
agent_relevance: Skill acts through both fast recognition and faster learning. Expect gains from stored knowledge even on poorly structured input.

source: Gobet & Simon (2000) Five seconds or sixty? CHREST simulation
finding: CHREST (EPAM-based, with templates) was run with no refit across time conditions. Nets of three sizes matched Class A, Expert and Master human data; logistic-fit r2 over .95.
numbers: Nets of 500, 10,000 and 300,000 nodes. Parameters: STM 3 visual chunks; discrimination 8 s; familiarisation 2 s; slot fill 250 ms; STM encode 50 ms; visual field +-2 squares; template if >3 nodes share information and chunk has >=5 elements. Tested on 50 game and 50 random positions per time.
limits: Model underestimates human Masters on game positions. Net size chosen to match 5 s recall (two degrees of freedom lost per net).
agent_relevance: A fully specified, parameter-fixed memory simulator. Parameters can be borrowed to size an agent's memory.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of random and distorted chess positions
finding: Mirror-image reflection around the vertical axis hurt recall more than horizontal reflection, so chunks encode specific piece-and-square patterns. This rejects location-free chunks and supports about 50,000 chunks.
numbers: N=25 (Masters 5, Experts 11, Class A 9). Normal+horizontal: Masters 77.3%, Experts 49.7%, Class A 34.5%; vertical+central: 62.9%, 38.6%, 27.5%. Skill x position type F(2,22)=3.48, p<.05. Simulation up to 70,000 nodes: normal 65.4% vs horizontal 63.2% (F(1,13)=19.8); vertical 53.3%, central 52.5%; delta 11.4%.
limits: Effect is modest; Holding's SEEK could explain it as harder-to-use schemas. Simulation used a simplified chunking model.
agent_relevance: Retrieval keyed on exact surface form is brittle to transformations. Memory cues must tolerate paraphrase.

source: Gobet (1998) Expert memory: a comparison of four theories
finding: Compared chunking, SEEK (Holding), long-term working memory (Ericsson & Kintsch) and template theory on random, distorted, short-presentation and interference data. Chunking fits more than critics claimed; templates fit best.
numbers: Multi-board limit about four or five boards at ~60% accuracy; exceptions: one Cooke et al. subject recalled 7 of 9 boards; the trained subject recalled 9 at >70% (160 pieces). Holding: 2,500 chunks vs Simon & Gilmartin 50,000.
limits: Author is a template-theory proponent. Long-term working memory is stronger for tasks with controlled retrieval structures.
agent_relevance: Prefer a model that combines low-level units with schema slots over pure schema or pure chunk views.

source: Gobet (1998) Memory for the meaningless: how chunks help
finding: CHREST matches the skill effect with random chess positions: the net holds small patterns that appear by chance. Model supports a visual STM of three or four chunks.
numbers: Human random-position recall at <=10 s pooled (Gobet & Simon 1995): Class A 11.7%, Experts 17.0%, Masters 23.7%. CHREST nets of 1k, 10k, 100k nodes without slots: 10.5%, 15.6%, 20.3%.
limits: Largest-chunk correlations with humans were low (0.20, 0.27, 0.03).
agent_relevance: Even scrambled material gets some help from many small stored fragments.

source: Gobet & Waters (2003) The role of constraints in expert memory
finding: Tested template theory vs the constraint attunement hypothesis (CAH) with truly random positions. CAH predicts no skill effect there; template theory predicts a small one. A small reliable skill effect remained.
numbers: N=36 players. Truly random recall: 14.8% (SD 5.14), 16.3, 13.7, 12.0 from strongest to weakest group; skill r=.34, p<.025. Skill slope 0.052 (SE .016) per BCF point vs template theory prediction 0.061. Sixteen CHREST nets (100-300,000 nodes), no parameters refit. Model overestimated human recall by 12.1% on average.
limits: Effect small; skill explains about 10% of variance for truly random positions; motivation and age confounds were checked and not supported.
agent_relevance: Chunk theory predicts a graded, small advantage on unstructured input; a benchmark to separate memory from reasoning.

source: Gobet & Jackson (2001) In search of templates
finding: Two subjects trained over 15 sessions to memorise chess positions. Recall and chunk size follow power functions of practice, as template theory predicts. CHREST reproduced the pattern but underestimated chunk size and learning rate.
numbers: N=2. Power fits: largest chunk 39*N^.31 (r2=.93) for CE and 55*N^.23 (r2=.81) for JD. Chunk count stayed at 3 or below. CHREST after 15 sessions: 4,772 chunks and 107 templates (CE); 5,811 chunks and 111 templates (JD). About half of subject chunks of 4+ pieces matched CHREST templates.
limits: N=2; conference paper; template matching is post hoc.
agent_relevance: Learning curves are power-law: early gains fast, later slow. Plan memory growth and evaluation accordingly.

source: Gobet (1997) A pattern-recognition theory of search in expert problem solving
finding: Templates can guide search: a model (SEARCH) built on CHREST predicts depth of search rising as a power function of net size, matching the small skill gap in human depth.
numbers: Mean depth: below 1 ply with no chunks, ~2.5 plies with 1,000 chunks, ~4 plies with ~30,000, over 5 plies with >100,000. Human data: de Groot Experts 4.8 and GMs 5.3 plies; Charness regression 2.3 (1300 Elo), 4.1 (2000), 5.7.
limits: Simulation, not tested on a new human sample here.
agent_relevance: Pattern memory shortens search. Link to pruning and recognition-primed decisions (other E16 subfields).

source: Smith, Lane & Gobet (2007) Modelling the relationship between visual STM capacity and recall ability
finding: Varied CHREST's STM capacity and presentation time. Only STM capacity produced the age x time interaction seen by Charness. A capacity of about four chunks was best; larger capacity gave little extra with big nets.
numbers: Nets up to 300,000 nodes (master level). Fit rose from 0.914 to 0.985 between STM capacity 3 and 4 and was best at 4. Six CHREST parameters tested.
limits: Chess only; authors warn against general conclusions.
agent_relevance: A small working set (about 4 units) suffices when long-term chunks are rich. Spend effort on the long-term store.

source: Jones, Gobet & Pine (2007) Computer simulations of developmental change: working memory capacity and long-term knowledge
finding: EPAM-VOC, an EPAM-style model of children's nonword repetition, varies knowledge and WM capacity separately. Knowledge growth alone fits child data; adding WM growth gives no significant gain.
numbers: WM duration of about 2,000-2,100 ms gave low RMSE (stage 7, 87.5% of input, RMSE about 8.9). Ages 2-3 and 4-5 compared.
limits: Phonological task, not chess; model-fit logic, not a causal manipulation.
agent_relevance: Knowledge, not raw capacity, drives gains. Supports spending on memory content, not a larger context.

source: Chassy, Lahaye & Gobet (2023) Templates but not emotions facilitate working memory
finding: Sternberg memory scan of 3, 4 or 5 chess positions (5 s each): experts were more accurate and faster than club players even with more stored content. Emotion priming did not reach significance.
numbers: N=60 (30 club, 30 expert). 5 s per board, 200 ms mask, 2 s emotion image. Priming ANOVAs ns (e.g. F(2,53)=0.63); experts rated less positive than club players (5.99 vs 6.68, p=.02).
limits: Emotion manipulation is weak. Cell means are noisy; the abstract's expert-speed claim is the main result.
agent_relevance: Rich structured stores speed scanning rather than slow it. Supports indexing over a large memory.

source: Lane & Gobet (2011) Perception in chess and beyond: commentary on Linhares & Freitas
finding: Reply to a critique that chunk models rely on surface similarity. Authors say the criticism of Chase & Simon is wrong, cite many results for location-specific encoding, and note CHREST already has similarity links.
numbers: No new data; cites location-specific encoding experiments (mirror image and quadrant swaps).
limits: Position paper; the critics' alternative (analogy-based 'experience recognition') is not tested head to head.
agent_relevance: A live objection: pure surface chunks do not capture analogy. The agent's memory should combine surface keys with relational descriptors.

source: Bennett & Gobet (2025) CogAct: concept learning by chunking
finding: A chunking model, CogAct, learns categories from raw text, chess and music with the same mechanisms and no hand-made features. It was compared with a neural baseline and with human subjective music judgments.
numbers: Chess opening categorisation (French vs Sicilian) about 85%, similar to CHREST with hand-made features (Lane & Gobet 2012). Human raters gave 100% confidence on 40 of 122 ratings; CogAct never did; the ANN twice.
limits: Preprint; supervised labels; far fewer chunks than the 300,000 estimated for chess masters.
agent_relevance: Chunking can be a domain-general learning step without feature engineering. Candidate for a light store inside a scaffold.

source: Feigenbaum & Simon (1984) EPAM-like models of recognition and learning (as described in Gobet & Simon 2000)
finding: EPAM grows a discrimination net by two operations: discrimination (adds a test and node when two objects differ) and familiarisation (adds features to an existing image). Taken from descriptions, not read in full.
numbers: Time costs used in later work: about 8 s per discrimination, 2 s per familiarisation, 50 ms to place a chunk in STM.
limits: Not opened; values as quoted by Gobet & Simon (2000).
agent_relevance: A concrete learning rule for a keyed memory: split a node only on observed mismatch.

source: Richman, Staszewski & Simon (1995) Simulation of expert memory using EPAM IV (as cited by Gobet & Simon 1996, 2000)
finding: EPAM IV simulated trained digit-span expert memory with a retrieval structure; its parameters (STM about 3-4 chunks, slot filling) were reused for CHREST.
numbers: STM of three visual chunks chosen from Zhang & Simon (1985) and Richman et al. (1995).
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: The same chunk-and-structure mechanism covers digit span and chess.

source: Lane & Gobet (2012) Using chunks to categorise chess positions (as cited by Bennett & Gobet 2025)
finding: CHREST categorised chess openings with hand-made attention heuristics at about 85% accuracy.
numbers: ~85% French vs Sicilian.
limits: Not opened; reported second-hand.
agent_relevance: Baseline for chunk-based classification of structured states.

source: Holding (1985, 1992) SEEK and the 2,500-chunk claim (as tested in Gobet 1998 and Gobet & Simon 1996)
finding: Holding argued that if chunks ignore colour and location, only about 2,500 are needed, not 50,000. Mirror-image and quadrant-swap tests (Gobet & Simon 1996; Saariluoma 1994) reduced recall, arguing against location-free chunks.
numbers: 2,500 vs 50,000 chunks. Recall loss modest for horizontal mirror, larger for vertical.
limits: Competing explanation: harder-to-use schemas. Holding's papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Counter-view: abstract schemas could shrink the store. Worth testing for an agent memory.
